Server-Side Development with Flask

Explore how Python on a server receives HTTP requests, runs logic, and returns dynamic HTML using Flask and Jinja2. This chapter teaches routing, handling GET and POST, template rendering, and processing form data.

Install Flask, create app.py, and run a local server.

Request → Process → Response

screens.title: Client-side vs Server-side
screens.narratorSegment: Let's define client-side and server-side code precisely and why the distinction matters. Client-side code—H T M L, C S S, and JavaScript—runs inside the user's browser. It controls structure, presentation, and immediate interactivity. Server-side code runs on a server machine and handles tasks that should not be exposed to the user: persistent storage, user authentication, sensitive business rules, and operations that require access to protected resources. For example, when a user logs in, the browser can collect credentials, but the server must check those credentials against stored data and issue a session or token; doing that check in the browser would expose secrets and be insecure. A common misconception is thinking server code is slower; in reality, server code allows centralized control and secure access to data. Another mistake is putting all validation in the browser—client-side checks improve UX but should never replace server-side validation. To ground this, imagine a message board: the browser can present a form to write a message, but the server receives the submitted text, stores it persistently, and returns an updated page. Key takeaway: server-side code is the authoritative gatekeeper for data and security. How will you separate concerns in your next project?

keyIdea.title: Separation of concerns
keyIdea.text: Client for presentation and experience; server for persistence, secrets, and authoritative logic.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Client vs Server
Definition

Client-side and Server-side

Client-side code runs in the browser for structure, style, and immediate interaction. Server-side code runs on a remote machine and handles secure operations, data persistence, and the generation of dynamic content.

Example: A login form is shown by the client; credentials are verified on the server before granting access.
Misconception: Client validation is sufficient. No — always validate on the server too.
Key Takeaway

Server code is the trusted place for storing data and enforcing security policies.

Analogy
Think of the client as a storefront window and the server as the store's inventory room and manager. The window shows items and accepts purchase requests; the manager checks inventory, records sales, and updates stock behind the scenes.
When to use server code: data storage, access control, complex calculations you do not want exposed to users.
When to use client code: instant UI feedback, DOM updates, and simple validation for user experience.
Practical example: a message board where posted messages are stored by the server so all visitors see the same list.

screens.title: HTTP Request-Response and Methods
screens.narratorSegment: HTTP is the protocol that lets a browser and server exchange data. A client makes a request; the server returns a response. Two HTTP methods matter most for simple apps: GET to retrieve resources and POST to submit data. When you type a URL or click a link, the browser sends a GET request asking the server for a page or resource. If form fields are placed on a page and the form uses GET, the data is appended to the URL as query parameters. That is useful for bookmarking or sharing a search, but it exposes data in the URL and is limited for sensitive content. A POST request submits data in the request body; the server reads it from the request object. POST is appropriate for login forms or when you create or modify resources. A common misconception is that GET is always safe; sometimes GET requests can change server state if endpoints are poorly designed. To practice, design routes so GET fetches and POST modifies, and test how form data appears in your server logs. Understanding these methods helps you choose safe defaults for building forms and APIs.

keyIdea.title: GET vs POST
keyIdea.text: Use GET to retrieve resources and keep responses bookmarkable; use POST to send sensitive or large data in the request body.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › HTTP Methods
Process

Request → Server → Response

  1. Step 1: Browser sends an HTTP request to a server.
  2. Step 2: Server inspects the method and path, runs matching code, and may read data from the request body or query string.
  3. Step 3: Server returns an HTTP response containing HTML, JSON, or a redirect.
GET: retrieve data; parameters appear in the URL; bookmarkable and visible.
POST: submit data in the body; suitable for forms and sensitive data.
Concrete Example
Search page uses GET so results and filters live in the URL. A login form should use POST so passwords are sent in the request body, not in the URL.
Common mistake
Treating GET as harmless. If a GET route modifies server state, you break assumptions about caching and bookmarking. Design your routes so GET is safe and POST performs modifications.
Key Takeaway

Choose GET for readable queries and POST for sending data that should not appear in the URL.

screens.title: Introducing Flask
screens.narratorSegment: Flask is a microframework for Python that gives you the basic building blocks to create web applications without imposing a large structure. It is intentionally minimal so you can choose additional libraries as needed. To begin, install Flask with pip and use a virtual environment to keep dependencies isolated. The install step is simply the pip install command in your terminal. Once installed, you create an app instance using the Flask class and define routes with decorators. A common beginner step is running the app locally in debug mode so the server restarts on changes and provides helpful traces. However, remember that debug mode should be turned off in production to avoid exposing sensitive information. Because Flask does not hide framework mechanics, you learn how requests map to functions, how to return strings or rendered templates, and how to inspect the request object. This directness makes Flask a great tool for learning server-side concepts while building practical projects like our message board. Introducing Flask means a small, flexible framework that maps urls to python functions and uses jinja2 for templates.. In practical terms, a lightweight python web framework. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Minimal Flask app

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › app.py Walkthrough
Example app.py
# app.py
from flask import Flask

app = Flask(__name__)

@app.route('/')
def index():
  return "Hello from Flask!"

if __name__ == '__main__':
  app.run(debug=True)
Walkthrough
  • Flask(): creates the application object used to register routes.
  • @app.route: decorator that binds a URL path to a function.
  • Return value: the function return is the HTTP response body.
  • app.run: starts a development server when the script runs directly.
Misconception: debug=True is fine for production. No — debug exposes internals and should be disabled in production.

screens.title: Dynamic Routes and URL Parameters
screens.narratorSegment: Flask routes can capture parts of the URL and pass them into your function as parameters. This allows you to build dynamic paths like a personalized greet route. The route path uses angled brackets to name a variable segment; Flask extracts that part of the URL and injects it into your view function argument. For example, navigating to greet slash Alice will call a function with name equal to Alice and return a greeting string that includes that value. This pattern is useful for user-specific pages, resource lookups by ID, and readable URLs. A common misconception is that URL parameters must be query strings; path parameters are part of the path and often more semantically meaningful. You should still validate or sanitize values from the URL before using them in sensitive operations. As a quick exercise, add a greet route to your app, visit URLs with different names, and observe how the returned text changes dynamically. Dynamic Routes and URL Parameters means use path parameters (e.g., /greet/<name>) to accept variable input directly in the url and pass it to your view function.. In practical terms, capture values from the url path. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Dynamic Routes
Example
@app.route('/greet/<name>')
def greet(name):
  return f"Hello, {name}!"
Visit /greet/Alice to see a personalized response. Flask passes Alice as the name argument to the function.
Usage notes
  • Path parameters are part of the URL and are good for readable addresses.
  • Validate path data before using it to query databases or run actions.
  • Prefer path parameters for identity and query strings for optional filters.
Check: try several names in the path to confirm dynamic behavior and think about edge cases like empty or malicious values.

keyIdea.text: Allow GET for showing forms and POST for processing them; always check request.method before accessing form data.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › GET & POST Handling
Login route (example)
@app.route('/login', methods=['GET', 'POST'])
def login():
  if request.method == 'POST':
    username = request.form['username']
    password = request.form['password']
    if username == 'admin' and password == 'password':
      return f"Welcome, {username}!"
    else:
      return "Invalid credentials."
  return '''
    <form method="post">
      <p><input type="text" name="username"></p>
      <p><input type="password" name="password"></p>
      <p><input type="submit" value="Login"></p>
    </form>
  '''
Explanation
  • The methods argument allows GET and POST on the same route.
  • Check request.method so you only access request.form when the form is submitted.
  • Return a rendered template or string depending on the outcome.
Common mistake: trying to read request.form on GET requests. Always branch on the method.

screens.title: The request Object and Form Data
screens.narratorSegment: Flask provides a request object that holds all incoming HTTP data for the current request. This includes query parameters, form data, headers, and the request method. When a form submits data via POST, the server can access the values through request. form using the field names. If you need optional fields, use request. form. get with a default value to avoid KeyError-like issues. Another part of requests is the query string accessible through request. args for GET parameters. Common mistakes include assuming form keys always exist or relying solely on client-side validation. Always validate and sanitize data you read from request before using it to update state or query a database. For example, when building a message board, read the message text and author fields from request. form, check that message_text is non-empty, and then append a structured dictionary to your messages list. This pattern keeps server logic predictable and avoids accepting malformed or empty submissions. The request Object and Form Data means access posted fields via request.form and get parameters via request.args; validate and handle optional fields gracefully.. In practical terms, how flask exposes incoming request information. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › render_template & redirect
Example snippet
@app.route('/')
def index():
  return render_template('index.html', title='Home Page', greeting='Welcome!', user='Cohortia Student')

@app.route('/submit', methods=['POST'])
def submit():
  # process data...
  return redirect(url_for('index'))
Why redirect?

Redirecting after POST converts the result into a GET request so refreshing won't repeat the form submission. url_for constructs the URL for a named view function, reducing hard-coded paths.

Developer tip

Use url_for('index') instead of '/': it adapts when you rename routes and avoids accidental broken links.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Message Board
Starter app.py
from flask import Flask, render_template, request, redirect, url_for

app = Flask(__name__)

messages = []

@app.route('/', methods=['GET', 'POST'])
def index():
  if request.method == 'POST':
    message_text = request.form['message_text']
    author_name = request.form.get('author_name', 'Anonymous')

    if message_text:
      messages.append({'text': message_text, 'author': author_name})
    return redirect(url_for('index'))

  return render_template('index.html', messages=messages)

if __name__ == '__main__':
  app.run(debug=True)
Starter templates/index.html
<h1>Simple Message Board</h1>

<form method="POST">
  <textarea name="message_text" placeholder="Your message..." required></textarea>
  <input type="text" name="author_name" placeholder="Your name (optional)">
  <input type="submit" value="Post Message">
</form>

<hr>

<h2>Messages</h2>
{% if messages %}
  {% for message in messages %}
    <div class="message">
      <p><strong>{{ message.author }}:</strong> {{ message.text }}</p>
    </div>
  {% endfor %}
{% else %}
  <p>No messages yet. Be the first to post!</p>
{% endif %}
Try this

Run the app, post messages, and confirm that redirect prevents duplicate posts on refresh.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's consolidate the most important ideas. First, server-side development runs code on the server to handle persistent storage, secrets, and authoritative logic—client-side code cannot securely perform these tasks. Second, HTTP methods matter: GET retrieves data and keeps parameters visible and bookmarkable, while POST sends data in the request body and is preferable for form submissions and sensitive content. Third, Flask maps URLs to Python functions via route decorators and uses the request object to give you access to form data and query parameters. Use these building blocks together: render_template to inject Python variables into Jinja2 templates, url_for to build routes safely, and redirect after POST to avoid duplicate submissions. As you build the message board, practice validating inputs, checking request. method before reading request. form, and keeping templates focused on presentation. These principles will guide you as you move from local development toward more complex server-side apps.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we move from code that runs in the browser to code that runs on a server. Server-side development is about receiving HTTP requests, running Python logic, and returning H T M L or data to the client. You will learn the difference between client-side and server-side work, how GET and POST shape communication, and how to build a small Flask app that serves dynamic pages. We'll install Flask, write an app file, add routes that accept parameters, render H T M L with Jinja2 templates, and process form submissions safely. By the end you'll have the mental model of the request-response cycle and a concrete message board example that stores messages in a list while you develop locally. This matters because persistent data, authentication, and controlled logic all require server-side code that you can test and secure. As you follow the code examples, notice common pitfalls like relying on raw returns for complex pages or failing to handle both GET and POST for forms. Ready to begin building a Flask app that bridges Python and the web?

Over the next screens you will build a clear mental model of server-side web development and gain hands-on skills. First, you'll understand the difference between code that runs in the browser and code that runs on a server. This distinction matters because only server-side code should handle persistent storage, authentication, or secrets. Second, you'll learn how HTTP methods shape interaction: when to use GET to request data and when to use POST to submit data. You'll practice both so you can choose appropriately. Third, you'll set up a minimal Flask app, learn how to define routes using decorators, and run a local development server. Finally, you'll render dynamic H T M L with Jinja2 and process form submissions on the server. Each objective includes a small mnemonic or visual hint to help you remember the workflow. These skills let you connect your front end to back-end logic safely and repeatedly. As you progress, compare GET and POST in real examples and notice how templates and request handling work together in the message board activity.

This checklist ties each objective to a concrete action so you can practice deliberately. For HTTP methods, show two examples: a search driven by GET with query parameters and a login form using POST. For Flask setup, create a project folder, use a virtual environment, install Flask, and run the app file to confirm the local server is reachable. For templating and form handling, build the message board: render an index template that displays messages and implement a POST route that adds a message to a list, then redirect to avoid re-submitting on refresh. Let's define client-side and server-side code precisely and why the distinction matters. Client-side code—H T M L, C S S, and JavaScript—runs inside the user's browser. It controls structure, presentation, and immediate interactivity. Server-side code runs on a server machine and handles tasks that should not be exposed to the user: persistent storage, user authentication, sensitive business rules, and operations that require access to protected resources. For example, when a user logs in, the browser can collect credentials, but the server must check those credentials against stored data and issue a session or token; doing that check in the browser would expose secrets and be insecure. A common misconception is thinking server code is slower; in reality, server code allows centralized control and secure access to data. Another mistake is putting all validation in the browser—client-side checks improve UX but should never replace server-side validation. Let's consolidate the most important ideas. First, server-side development runs code on the server to handle persistent storage, secrets, and authoritative logic—client-side code cannot securely perform these tasks. Second, HTTP methods matter: GET retrieves data and keeps parameters visible and bookmarkable, while POST sends data in the request body and is preferable for form submissions and sensitive content. Third, Flask maps URLs to Python functions via route decorators and uses the request object to give you access to form data and query parameters. Use these building blocks together: render_template to inject Python variables into Jinja2 templates, url_for to build routes safely, and redirect after POST to avoid duplicate submissions. These principles will guide you as you move from local development toward more complex server-side apps.

Before you code, keep three compact reminders in mind. One: separate concerns — UI in the client, data and secrets on the server. Two: pick the right HTTP method — GET for safe retrieval and bookmarkable queries, POST for sending form data or making changes. Three: use templates and the request object properly — render_template to pass data and request. form or request. args to read input, always validating what you receive. When you build features, follow the Post-Redirect-Get flow for form submissions so refreshes do not duplicate actions.
